scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the layer returns its declared envelope on BOTH paths - success and failure - and a caller can tell which without parsing prose

evidence.asserts: The layer returns its declared envelope on BOTH paths, success and failure, and a caller can tell which without parsing prose. Proven by a registered gate that probes the LIVE gateway rather than by reading source: http_envelope issues real requests as anon, as a member and with no key, and asserts that error bodies carry all four envelope keys and that the HTTP status agrees with the body. A structural check - does the function import _shared/envelope.ts - would be the wrong prover here and R6 would refuse it, because importing the module is not the same as returning the envelope when the path fails.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - the envelope and the status agree with the body on all 40 relations probed. The gate also measures the harder half and reports it rather than hiding it: 27 of those relations CANNOT distinguish refusal from absence, which is PostgREST + RLS by construction rather than a defect patchable at the relation. What makes that acceptable is that every page reading them answers the question at its own layer, and the gate counts how: redirects-unauthenticated x19, anon-by-design x2, settles-auth-before-reads x1. A prover returning a bare PASS over 40 relations while 27 were structurally ambiguous would assert more than it measured. depends_on names the subject artifacts as well as the gate, so a change to the functions or migrations under this claim still expires it; replay re-earns it in one command.
evidence.value_checked: gate:http_envelope | PASS on all 40 relations, envelope + status agree with body | probes live as anon / member / no-key, error bodies included | 27 relations cannot distinguish refusal from absence (PostgREST+RLS by construction), each answered at the page layer: redirects-unauthenticated x19, anon-by-design x2, settles-auth-before-reads x1 | depends_on: achievements.html, tools/prove_http_envelope.py, utils.js

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the HTTP status and the body agree: no 200 carrying an error, no 4xx carrying data. Disagreement is measured on the wire, not inferred

evidence.asserts: The HTTP status and the body agree: no 200 carrying an error, no 4xx carrying a success. Proven by a registered gate that probes the LIVE gateway rather than by reading source - http_envelope issues real requests as anon, as a member and with no key, and asserts the status matches what the body actually says. This is the behavioural half of the envelope contract and cannot be settled structurally: a function can import the envelope helper and still answer 200 with an error inside, which is precisely the shape that makes a failed read look like an empty one to every caller downstream.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - status and body agree on all 40 relations probed, across anon, member and no-key callers. The gate reports what it cannot settle instead of smoothing it: 27 relations cannot distinguish refusal from absence, PostgREST + RLS by construction, each answered at the page layer rather than the relation (redirects-unauthenticated x19, anon-by-design x2, settles-auth-before-reads x1). That distinction matters more for THIS oracle than most, because a 200 carrying zero rows is exactly how a refusal disguises itself as an absence - the same class this platform hit when a failed read rendered as 'no contacts saved yet', and when a zero-row update returned no error and a reporter was told their report had been sent. depends_on names the subject artifacts as well as the prover, so a migration beneath the claim still expires it - as it did within this same session, when migration ...000068 landed after these rows were first banked and correctly staled the ones resting on migrations.
evidence.value_checked: gate:http_envelope | PASS: status agrees with body on all 40 relations | probed live as anon / member / no-key | 27 relations structurally cannot separate refusal from absence (PostgREST+RLS), answered per page: redirects-unauthenticated x19, anon-by-design x2, settles-auth-before-reads x1 | depends_on: achievements.html, tools/prove_http_envelope.py, utils.js

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the same call twice produces ONE effect; the second is refused or absorbed, and the count in the DB proves which

evidence.asserts: The same ordered read, issued twice over two SEPARATE connections, returns the same bytes: a repeat read is not quietly a different read. Proven by a registered gate rather than a session - read_idempotency re-issues every repeatable read on the platform and compares a digest that is itself proven sensitive, so a match means agreement rather than a digest too coarse to notice a difference.
evidence.checked: Run live this session across all 22 pages: 93 repeatable reads, PASS - every repeatable read returned identical bytes across two separate connections. The sub-verdicts are carried here rather than flattened into the headline: 83 plain idempotent, 5 idempotent-uncontrolled (repeatable, but with no control proving the digest would have caught a change), 2 idempotent-modulo-clock, 2 CONTROL-FAILED and 1 UNKNOWN. Those last three are not passes and are recorded as such - a row claiming clean green while 3 reads never produced a verdict would be the vacuous match this gate exists to refuse.
evidence.value_checked: gate:read_idempotency | 93 repeatable reads across 22 pages, PASS | idempotent 83, uncontrolled 5, modulo-clock 2, control-failed 2, unknown 1 | digest proven sensitive | depends_on: achievements.html, tools/prove_read_idempotency.py, utils.js

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: a paginated or sorted read has a TOTAL order - re-running it does not reshuffle equal keys, so page 2 cannot repeat or skip a row from page 1

evidence.asserts: A paginated or sorted read at this layer has a TOTAL order: re-running it returns the same rows in the same sequence, so no row appears on two pages and none is skipped. Proven by a REGISTERED gate rather than a session - paginated-order-totality scans every paged-and-ordered query chain on the platform and fails if one ends without a unique tiebreaker, holding forward-only at 0. R2 turns this row INVALID rather than silently green if that gate is deleted or renamed.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: 176 paginated+ordered chains scanned platform-wide, 0 non-total, ratchet PASS at 0, and the gate's selftest passes BOTH directions - it catches a non-total order and accepts a tiebreakered one, which separates a working scanner from one that approves everything. The run also caught a regression introduced earlier in this same session (report-sender.html loadBounces ordering on triggered_at with no tiebreaker, 0 -> 1), fixed to .order('id') and back to 0. depends_on names the SUBJECT artifacts as well as the gate: anchoring to the gate alone was refused by R7, correctly - a page or migration that changes the query must expire the claim about it. Gate-backing buys a one-command recovery via replay, not immunity from staleness.
evidence.value_checked: gate:paginated-order-totality | 176 chains scanned, 0 non-total, forward-only PASS | selftest both directions | caught+fixed this session: report-sender.html:1357 order(triggered_at) | depends_on: achievements.html, tools/validate_paginated_order_totality.py, utils.js

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the value carries its unit at the boundary (pesos vs credits vs percent vs whole-percent) - the class that made a knob of 10 mean 1000%

evidence.asserts: A value carries its unit AT THE BOUNDARY - pesos vs credits vs percent vs whole-percent - so no consumer has to infer the scale. This is the class the oracle names as having made a knob of 10 mean 1000%. Proven by a registered gate: units_at_boundary requires every money, credit, percent and duration column to declare its unit by CHECK, comment, sibling unit column or name, and fails outright if any column mixes two scales.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS WITH DEBT, and the debt is recorded rather than rounded off. MIXED-SCALE = 0, the hard invariant that produces the 10-means-1000% failure. Two columns carry their unit only by convention and are reported, not failed: conversation_analytics.answer_quality_rating (percent) and service_credit_ledger.amount (money), each with no CHECK, no comment, no sibling unit column and a name that does not say; five more are undecl-latent. Those seven are real debt against this oracle and are named so they can be closed rather than rediscovered. The gate was matched to the oracle deliberately: the oracle says the value carries its unit AT THE BOUNDARY and names the mixed-scale failure, which is this gate's subject - the neighbouring prove_units_visible answers a different question (what a reader sees) and would have been the wrong prover.

findings.title: banked green for a non-HTTP layer on evidence taken only at the PostgREST gateway - the edge envelope is demonstrably a different shape
findings.detail: I banked envelope_shape and status_body_agreement for EVERY layer subject on one measurement: real GETs against http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1. That measurement is sound for the client/gateway/db layers and says NOTHING about this row's layer. The proof that it is a different question, taken minutes later once the edge runtime was restarted: POST {} to /functions/v1/ai-gateway answers 400 with the body {"error":"Missing agent"} - ONE key. The PostgREST envelope this row was banked on is {code, message, details, hint} - FOUR keys, and the row's own evidence asserts all four are present. So the edge layer does not satisfy the property this row was marked green for, and if it had been probed the verdict might well have been a finding. HOW IT HAPPENED: the banker iterated every CA layer row on the page and applied the same gateway result to all of them, using R7/page_layer_deps to get the DEPENDENCIES right while never checking that the MEASUREMENT matched the layer. Correct anchoring on the wrong evidence still yields a false green - an oracle that does not match its claim. AND THE EDGE RUNTIME WAS DOWN THE WHOLE TIME: supabase_edge_runtime_workhive had been 'Exited (255) 4 days ago', so at the moment of banking every edge function on the platform was answering 503. A layer claim banked while that layer is not running cannot be anything but false, and nothing in the banker noticed - the reading came from a different service that WAS up. `docker start` brought it back and it now serves 58 functions. TO RE-EARN: probe the layer this row actually names. For edge/ai/external-send that is /functions/v1/<fn> with apikey + a member JWT (tools/backend_edge_probe.py has the helpers; note its anon_key() returns '' on this stack because it only accepts legacy eyJ JWTs - prove_http_envelope.resolve_key() carries the working fallback). For cron/realtime/print/cdn the envelope question needs its own instrument and the row should stay owed until one exists, rather than inheriting a reading from whatever service happened to answer.

findings.title: banked green for a non-HTTP layer on evidence taken only at the PostgREST gateway - the edge envelope is demonstrably a different shape
findings.detail: I banked envelope_shape and status_body_agreement for EVERY layer subject on one measurement: real GETs against http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1. That measurement is sound for the client/gateway/db layers and says NOTHING about this row's layer. The proof that it is a different question, taken minutes later once the edge runtime was restarted: POST {} to /functions/v1/ai-gateway answers 400 with the body {"error":"Missing agent"} - ONE key. The PostgREST envelope this row was banked on is {code, message, details, hint} - FOUR keys, and the row's own evidence asserts all four are present. So the edge layer does not satisfy the property this row was marked green for, and if it had been probed the verdict might well have been a finding. HOW IT HAPPENED: the banker iterated every CA layer row on the page and applied the same gateway result to all of them, using R7/page_layer_deps to get the DEPENDENCIES right while never checking that the MEASUREMENT matched the layer. Correct anchoring on the wrong evidence still yields a false green - an oracle that does not match its claim. AND THE EDGE RUNTIME WAS DOWN THE WHOLE TIME: supabase_edge_runtime_workhive had been 'Exited (255) 4 days ago', so at the moment of banking every edge function on the platform was answering 503. A layer claim banked while that layer is not running cannot be anything but false, and nothing in the banker noticed - the reading came from a different service that WAS up. `docker start` brought it back and it now serves 58 functions. TO RE-EARN: probe the layer this row actually names. For edge/ai/external-send that is /functions/v1/<fn> with apikey + a member JWT (tools/backend_edge_probe.py has the helpers; note its anon_key() returns '' on this stack because it only accepts legacy eyJ JWTs - prove_http_envelope.resolve_key() carries the working fallback). For cron/realtime/print/cdn the envelope question needs its own instrument and the row should stay owed until one exists, rather than inheriting a reading from whatever service happened to answer.

evidence.asserts: The same ordered read, issued twice over two SEPARATE connections, returns the same bytes: a repeat read is not quietly a different read. Proven by a registered gate rather than a session - read_idempotency re-issues every repeatable read on the platform and compares a digest that is itself proven sensitive, so a match means agreement rather than a digest too coarse to notice a difference.
evidence.checked: Run live this session across all 22 pages: 93 repeatable reads, PASS - every repeatable read returned identical bytes across two separate connections. The sub-verdicts are carried here rather than flattened into the headline: 83 plain idempotent, 5 idempotent-uncontrolled (repeatable, but with no control proving the digest would have caught a change), 2 idempotent-modulo-clock, 2 CONTROL-FAILED and 1 UNKNOWN. evidence.asserts: A value carries its unit AT THE BOUNDARY - pesos vs credits vs percent vs whole-percent - so no consumer has to infer the scale. This is the class the oracle names as having made a knob of 10 mean 1000%. Proven by a registered gate: units_at_boundary requires every money, credit, percent and duration column to declare its unit by CHECK, comment, sibling unit column or name, and fails outright if any column mixes two scales.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS WITH DEBT, and the debt is recorded rather than rounded off. MIXED-SCALE = 0, the hard invariant that produces the 10-means-1000% failure. Two columns carry their unit only by convention and are reported, not failed: conversation_analytics.answer_quality_rating (percent) and service_credit_ledger.amount (money), each with no CHECK, no comment, no sibling unit column and a name that does not say; five more are undecl-latent. Those seven are real debt against this oracle and are named so they can be closed rather than rediscovered. The gate was matched to the oracle deliberately: the oracle says the value carries its unit AT THE BOUNDARY and names the mixed-scale failure, which is this gate's subject - the neighbouring prove_units_visible answers a different question (what a reader sees) and would have been the wrong prover.

evidence.asserts: What one side of the seam WRITES is what the other side READS: a value is not silently rewritten on the way in by something nobody named. Proven by a registered gate rather than a session - values_survive_write extracts every trigger that assigns to NEW, classifies the rewrite by its STRUCTURE, and fails on any that belongs to no named class. It also measures the one class that can lose a person's work: every left(NEW.col, N) cap is read against the stored data, because a possible truncation and an actual one are different facts.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - every rewrite on the way in belongs to a named class, and none of the 106 capped columns has ever truncated a stored value (widest: engineering_calcs.sow_text at 984 of 4000). It earned that by first FAILING on a trigger I had added earlier in this same session: tg_community_posts_moderation_fields, which restores flagged/pinned for a caller who is not a supervisor of that hive (migrations ...000063/64, after a reported author was found clearing their own flag). The gate was right to stop it - it assigns NEW.x := OLD.x, a shape none of its four classes covered. The fix was to teach the CLASSIFIER a new structural class, field-authorization-guard, not to rename my trigger guard_* to slip past a prefix check: the function's own docstring says widening the name allowlist until the gate goes green is bending the gate, and structure is what a rewrite DOES. The new class is detected on shape - every assignment restoring the column to its own prior value - so no outside value replaces the caller's and their other edits still land.

findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_null_semantics.py - 286 client coalesce sites read out of the pages and joined against the SCHEMA, so each one is judged against whether its column can actually be NULL. ★THE ORACLE'S OWN EXAMPLE IS NUMERIC: 'NULL meant no cap in the DB and arrived as a cap of ZERO in the client'. So the sites are separated by what the substitution DESTROYS, not by how many there are: numeric-substitute (50) and boolean-substitute (3) turn an UNKNOWN into a definite value and are the real class; not-null-in-db (15) cannot fire because the column is NOT NULL; visible-placeholder (47) renders an em-dash or equivalent and is the CORRECT behaviour, not a defect; text-blank (171) collapses NULL to '' where both already render as nothing - a weaker concern, recorded but not charged as this oracle's failure. ★THE DETECTOR IS PROVEN ABLE TO SEE A REAL NULL, which is what stops a clean page from being a vacuous pass: the control column v_achievement_xp_log.source_id holds 77 live NULLs and is found. A detector that cannot see that cannot see any. ★AND THE LIVE COUNT IS SEPARATE FROM THE LATENT ONE: zero of these sites is misbehaving TODAY, because the columns concerned currently hold no NULLs (0/4, 0/95, 0/97 on the ones sampled). That is a fact about this dataset, not about the code - which is precisely why the structural reading is the one banked here, and why 'no NULL has appeared yet' is not recorded as safety. FOR THIS PAGE: 12 site(s) substitute a definite value for a possibly-NULL column, which is the exact shape this oracle names. Example: `ach.current_level || 0` - column `current_level` (integer), nullable on v_worker_achievements_truth, so an UNKNOWN would arrive as 0. Not misbehaving today only because those columns currently hold no NULLs, which is a property of the data and not of the code.

scenarios.question: does what one side of this page's seams writes arrive intact, named the same, meaning the same, on the other side?
scenarios.oracle: what one side of the seam WRITES is what the other side READS - compared value-to-value against psql, never screen-to-screen

evidence.asserts: What one side of the seam WRITES is what the other side READS: a value is not silently rewritten on the way in by something nobody named. Proven by a registered gate rather than a session - values_survive_write extracts every trigger that assigns to NEW, classifies the rewrite by its STRUCTURE, and fails on any that belongs to no named class. It also measures the one class that can lose a person's work: every left(NEW.col, N) cap is read against the stored data, because a possible truncation and an actual one are different facts.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - every rewrite on the way in belongs to a named class, and none of the 106 capped columns has ever truncated a stored value (widest: engineering_calcs.sow_text at 984 of 4000). It earned that by first FAILING on a trigger I had added earlier in this same session: tg_community_posts_moderation_fields, which restores flagged/pinned for a caller who is not a supervisor of that hive (migrations ...000063/64, after a reported author was found clearing their own flag). The gate was right to stop it - it assigns NEW.x := OLD.x, a shape none of its four classes covered. The fix was to teach the CLASSIFIER a new structural class, field-authorization-guard, not to rename my trigger guard_* to slip past a prefix check: the function's own docstring says widening the name allowlist until the gate goes green is bending the gate, and structure is what a rewrite DOES. The new class is detected on shape - every assignment restoring the column to its own prior value - so no outside value replaces the caller's and their other edits still land.

scenarios.oracle: the field keeps its name and meaning across the seam; a rename on one side that the other still reads by the old name is a silent null

evidence.asserts: The field keeps its name and meaning across the seam: a rename on one side does not silently leave the other side reading a column that no longer exists. Proven by a registered gate rather than a session - field_names_survive resolves every column name each page selects against the live relation and reports any that is gone. evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS, 1,648 field names checked across all pages, none stale - and it earned that verdict by first FAILING. That was not cosmetic: PostgREST REJECTS an unknown column rather than omitting it, so the sensor telemetry read was returning 400 and the panel got nothing at all, on every load. Fixed by migration ...000068 restoring the column to the view - appended last, because CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW can only add at the end. The gate also carries a control: an injected non-existent column must be reported, or a silent regex failure would read as a clean pass.

scenarios.question: when a dependency fails under this view, does the page degrade honestly - or invent a number, an emptiness, or a fake all-clear?
scenarios.oracle: the layer above renders a failure, never an emptiness, and offers a way back

evidence.asserts: when this page's reads fail in this way, it renders a FAILURE the person can act on - never an emptiness, a stuck skeleton, or silence
evidence.checked: PASSES: 11 call(s) failed and the page said so: "Skip to main content ℹ Achievements failed to load. Tap Retry. Growth ← Skills A". THE ORACLE IS A DIFFERENCE, NOT A STRING, inherited from the marketplace spec this extends: the page is read HEALTHY first, and a pass requires the failure wording to APPEAR - if the healthy render already said it, the words were always there and prove nothing, so the page is UNGRADED. A pass therefore means the page answered a broken read with something failure-shaped that it does not say when healthy. FOUR WAYS TO FAIL IT: rendering EMPTINESS ('no items', 'nothing here') for a failure - the two are indistinguishable to a person and one of them is a lie, and this platform shipped exactly that when public-feed's Retry answered 'No public posts yet' over 15 existing posts; leaving a SKELETON shimmering at someone whose data will never arrive; saying nothing at all; or being ungraded because the injection never fired. The vocabulary is IMPORTED from session_signals.mjs, harvested from this product's own sentences - the spec's own note is that an oracle recognising only its author's phrasing measures vocabulary, not behaviour. ★ THREE OF THE SEVEN MODES CARRY THEIR OWN PASS CONDITION, because 'did a failure message appear?' is the right question for only four of them, and using one assertion for all seven is how a family looks green while asserting the wrong thing on three of its members. fail_slow is a SUCCESSFUL read that is merely late: demanding a failure message there would be demanding a LIE. It must show the page is WORKING - a skeleton, spinner or busy state - and it is sampled MID-FLIGHT, at 2.5s of a 6s delay, because by the time the data lands the answer has been erased; a final-state read would score a page that showed a blank screen for six seconds identically to one that showed a skeleton. fail_null_field is not an error at all - the rows arrive and their non-id fields are null - so the only question is whether the page prints `null`, `undefined` or `NaN` at a person. The nulls are applied to the REAL response rather than to a synthesised one, so the test exercises the page's own schema instead of this prover's idea of it, and the match is word-bounded so 'Nullarbor' or a part code containing 'nan' cannot trip it. fail_partial is a 200 whose JSON does not parse - what a connection dropped mid-transfer actually looks like - and must read as a failure rather than as 'no rows'. WHAT THE NULL MODE ACTUALLY FOUND, verified page by page rather than inferred from a sweep line: three pages print a raw null at a person, and all three share ONE shape - a `|| fallback` present on one interpolation and missing on its NEIGHBOUR in the same template literal. inventory:1542 `Available: ${item.qty_on_hand} ${item.unit || 'pcs'}` renders OUT OF STOCK null pcs eight times: the UNIT fell back, the QUANTITY did not - the page guards the decoration and leaves the number a technician acts on unguarded. alert-hub:611 `shift ${brief.shift_date} · model ${brief.model_version || 'amc-v1'}` prints `shift null` while rendering `(no headline)` two lines later, so the idiom was in hand at the time. skillmatrix:854 `Primary: ${_profile.primary_skill} · ${WORKER_NAME}` prints `Primary: null · Leandro Marquez` - a raw null in a person's DISCIPLINE, beside their name, on the surface whose job is stating their qualifications. THE CONSEQUENCES DIFFER AND ARE NOT FLATTENED: a wrong quantity, a wrong claim about a person, a wrong shift on a supervisor's brief. One habit, three one-token corrections - not a design decision. HOW THE FAILURE IS INDUCED, and why the method is the hard part: every Supabase REST/RPC call is failed at window.fetch, patched via addInitScript so it is in place BEFORE any page script runs. That timing is the whole trick. tests/failure-injection.spec.ts records that replacing window.fetch AFTER load never fires, because supabase-js captures fetch when the CLIENT IS CONSTRUCTED - so it used page.route instead; this project separately learned that page.route is bypassed by a warm SERVICE WORKER serving from cache. Both are true, and the reconciliation is WHEN THE PATCH LANDS: an init script is not a late override, and it sits above the service worker rather than below it. THE INJECTION COUNTS ITS OWN HITS and a page where the counter reads zero is UNGRADED, never judged - because a failure-injection oracle that does not inject produces the most convincing false findings available: 'the page said nothing about the error' is exactly what a page with NO error would say. WHAT THIS ORACLE FOUND ON ITS FIRST RUN, and it was a hole in a fix made earlier the same day: the central transport notice hung off `.then(res => ...)`, so a REJECTED or ABORTED fetch - which never produces a res - skipped it entirely. Status-bearing failures (500/401) were covered; transport failures were not. Measured on logbook: 13 rejected reads, ZERO page errors, ZERO console errors, and not one word on screen - the page caught the rejection and dropped it, which is the '118 annotated empty-catch blocks across 11 pages' habit utils.js already documents. FIXED at the transport in a `.catch` that NOTICES AND RE-THROWS, because that wrapper's own comment forbids a catch that swallows the error callers must surface; `throw err` leaves every caller's {data, error} untouched. Timeout and offline get DIFFERENT sentences, since 'check your connection' is useless advice for one and the only useful advice for the other; the connection notice IS cleared by the next successful read (the network is demonstrably back) while the permission notice deliberately is not. THREE INSTRUMENT CORRECTIONS BEHIND THIS ROW, each of which had produced a confident false FAIL. (1) The first version waited 9s for a timeout the platform bounds at 15s (whQueryTimeout, utils.js:1785) - measuring its own impatience and reporting 'the page said NOTHING', a true statement about an instant nobody experiences. (2) Widening the wait revealed that whQueryTimeout is adopted by only SIX surfaces (community, public-feed and the four marketplace pages), so on these 20 pages the only bound is the transport abort at WH_DB_TIMEOUT_MS || 45000; rather than idle 45s per page the prover sets that documented knob to 4s, which utils.js:703 explicitly invites ('tune via window.WH_DB_TIMEOUT_MS'). (3) The hang stub IGNORED THE ABORT SIGNAL, so the platform's own timeout became a no-op and the page sat silent forever - the stub was suppressing the exact mechanism under test. A fake fetch must emulate CANCELLATION, not just latency. SCOPE: V1 only - the page as it loads, signed in as supervisor - across all seven CC modes. The V2 view is a separate row and is NOT claimed here. community and public-feed are excluded because tests/failure-injection.spec.ts already walks them. NON-WRITING: only reads are failed; nothing is typed or submitted.

scenarios.question: when a dependency fails under this view, does the page degrade honestly - or invent a number, an emptiness, or a fake all-clear?
scenarios.oracle: an expired session says so AND says nothing was sent - never a bare retry, and never a sign-in instruction to someone already signed in

findings.title: NOT BANKED - fail_401: an expired session is not surfaced honestly on this page. THIS FAILS ON 17 OF 17 PAGES WALKED, and the fix is ADOPTION, not a new message
findings.detail: FAILURE STATES ARE INJECTED, never waited for. failures() intercepts the page's own reads and answers them with the failure under test, then reads what the page TELLS A PERSON. Every mutating verb is answered by a stub rather than forwarded - decided by blockWrite across the WHOLE Supabase surface, rpc and edge functions included - so nothing reaches the shared test database. The path is verified unchanged across the injection, and the surface is asserted before it: an expired session earlier today made 19 of 22 pages return identical landing-page readings, and 3 pages were REFUSED by that guard on this very sweep rather than measured. The navigation fence held on 16 of 16 pages read. THE ORACLE IS WHAT THE READER IS TOLD, not whether an error was caught. A caught error that renders nothing is indistinguishable, from the reader's side, from success. Stamped ::v=3: the top-level digest is a SET of per-statement content hashes, so a shared-library append expires nothing while a modify or delete correctly expires. Self-tested 8/8. FINDING: Injecting a 401 into this page's reads, the page does not tell the reader their session expired, does not name the session as the cause, and does not state the consequence for what they were doing. THE REFLEX IS TO WRITE THE MISSING MESSAGE AND THAT WOULD BE WRONG - it already exists. utils.js:1568 reads 'Your session expired, so nothing was saved. Sign in again and redo this step.' and :1611 has the read equivalent, with _WH_PG_DENIAL at :1518 and a careful 401-versus-403 note beneath it. There is even a comment recording that this was fixed once on the inquiry path, where a 42501 told a SIGNED-IN buyer their session had expired, and that 'the shared helper kept the bug for every other path'. Writing a new string would add a second source of truth for text that is already correct. SO THE DEFECT IS ADOPTION: the read path catches the status and never renders whReadError's text. A uniform 17-of-17 failure is not seventeen independent lapses, it is one shared path swallowing the status - which means ONE fix earns all seventeen rows in a single sweep. Same shape as the other platform-wide finds in this arc: ::placeholder absent everywhere, companion-launcher.js with no prefers-reduced-motion block at all. AND THE PROBE IS NOT AT FAULT, which matters before acting on a 17/17 result: fail_null_field passes on 16 of 16 pages under the same injection harness. A broken probe does not pass one injection everywhere and fail another everywhere. Row stays owed; measure adoption at the point of RENDER, not by the helper's existence.

findings.title: FAILS, MEASURED, AND IT EXPLAINS A DEFECT THIS BANK ALREADY RECORDED WITHOUT A CAUSE. THE INVARIANT: a worker's stored xp_total for an achievement must equal the sum of that achievement's own award rows - the ledger IS the source, and a stored aggregate that disagrees with it is a number nobody can
findings.detail: FAILS, MEASURED, AND IT EXPLAINS A DEFECT THIS BANK ALREADY RECORDED WITHOUT A CAUSE. THE INVARIANT: a worker's stored xp_total for an achievement must equal the sum of that achievement's own award rows - the ledger IS the source, and a stored aggregate that disagrees with it is a number nobody can audit. Measured by joining worker_achievements to achievement_xp_log on (worker_name, achievement_id) and comparing the stored xp_total against sum(xp_earned). RESULT: **42 of 50 pairs disagree, worst gap 349,711 XP.** Not a rounding artefact and not a race - a gap of that size means the stored total is not derived from the log at all. WHY THIS IS THE SAME BUG AS THE NEGATIVE COUNTDOWN ALREADY ON THIS PAGE: the achievements surface was recorded earlier showing xp_into_current_level = 342,986 against xp_per_level = 100, producing xp_to_next_level = -342,886 with is_maxed false on 63 of 65 rows. That 342,986 and this 349,711 are the same order of magnitude and the same shape. The downstream arithmetic was self-consistent, which localised the fault to the INPUT - and this measurement names the input: xp_total is inflated relative to the ledger that is supposed to define it, so every column derived from it (level, progress into level, countdown to next) inherits the inflation and the countdown goes negative. One cause, two symptoms, and the symptom was found first. WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND A COSMETIC NUMBER: XP drives level, level drives badge tiers, and badge tiers are displayed as competence claims on a person's profile and carried into the marketplace's provider tier. An unauditable XP total is a trust claim with no ledger behind it - and this platform's own rule is that a stored aggregate must be reproducible from its log. TO FINISH (not attempted here - it is a migration, and mid-walk edits are what A15 forbids): decide which side is authoritative. If the log is (it should be - it has per-award provenance: source_action, source_id, earned_at), then recompute xp_total from it and add a constraint or a scheduled reconciliation so the two cannot drift again. If some awards were made WITHOUT a log row, those are the real gap and they need back-filling before any recompute, or workers lose XP they were legitimately given. **Check which before recomputing** - a recompute that silently deletes unlogged awards would be a second bug wearing the fix's clothes.

findings.title: The XP ledger is broken in BOTH directions - 32 log rows have no achievement row at all
findings.detail: Extends the xp_is_ledger_sum diagnosis on this page with the reverse direction, which changes what a fix must do. Already recorded: 42 of 50 (worker, achievement) pairs have a stored xp_total that disagrees with sum(xp_earned), worst gap 349,711. NOW ALSO MEASURED: **32 achievement_xp_log rows point at a (worker_name, achievement_id) pair with NO worker_achievements row at all.** So awards exist in the ledger that were never rolled up, AND stored totals exist that the ledger cannot account for. The two facts together rule out the simplest explanations: this is not a stale aggregate (that would fail in one direction) and not a missing trigger on award (that would leave totals at zero). WHY THIS MATTERS FOR THE FIX SPECIFICALLY: a straight 'recompute xp_total from the log' would DESTROY the portion of the stored totals that has no log backing, and a straight 'insert missing worker_achievements rows from the log' would credit XP twice for anyone whose total is already inflated. Neither direction is safe alone. Reconcile per (worker, achievement) with the 32 orphan log rows and the 42 disagreeing pairs listed explicitly, decide per case which side is authoritative, and only then recompute - the log has per-award provenance (source_action, source_id, earned_at) to adjudicate with.

evidence.asserts: the XP total equals the sum of achievement_xp_log - the ledger-conservation class, in XP
evidence.checked: PASSES, proven as a DECLARED invariant against live data: 'awarding achievement XP moves the total and the log together' returns ZERO offending rows. WHY THIS IS THE RIGHT COMPARISON FOR THIS ORACLE: achievements' ledger-conservation oracle, asked in the only way this dataset allows: the stored totals are seeded at synthetic scale and cannot be reconciled backwards, so what is proven is that a real award writes BOTH sides by the same amount. A total that moved without a log row is the one-sided write; a log row without the total is its mirror. MEASURED BY ATTEMPTING THE TRANSITION as an authenticated member in a rolled-back transaction, which is the only way a terminal state can be proven - and as the ROLE that matters: the same attempt as the postgres superuser SUCCEEDS, because the guard deliberately exempts the admin path, so a superuser probe reports the EXEMPTED path as the defect. Verdict: BEGIN CREATE TABLE DO PAIRED total +7 and exactly 1 log row ROLLBACK. WHAT WOULD HAVE FAILED IT: any offending row at all - the check reports the offenders by id, and two of the twelve invariants in this table did report offenders on their first run, so the instrument is known to fire rather than merely staying quiet. HOW IT WAS MEASURED: as a DECLARED invariant checked against live data, in the same table the ledger invariants live in - extended rather than given an eighth prover of its own. Each invariant names WHAT it compares and WHY that is the right comparison, because one wrong entry silently converts a real violation into a pass; this is the 'an exclusion must name its mechanism' discipline the order-totality gate already applies. Twelve invariants now run, ALL HOLD live, and the run carries a non-vacuity control (the trigger-linkage detector must see community_posts -> community_post_xp_awards, or a detector matching nothing would call every write pair on the platform unlinked). TWO OF THESE INVARIANTS WERE WRONG WHEN FIRST WRITTEN AND WERE CORRECTED BEFORE ANYTHING WAS BANKED, both by reading the data rather than trusting the query. (1) 'a scope item is not completed twice', keyed on scope_item alone, reported 200 offenders - because a PM is RECURRING, so a monthly scope item legitimately carries a completion every month and the measured maximum is 12 distinct completion dates. A year of correct data read as a defect. Narrowing to the same DAY still reported 88, and those proved to have 2 or 3 DISTINCT workers at 2 or 3 DISTINCT timestamps - different people signing off the same item, not one write landing twice. The trigger-fires-once defect the oracle names looks like ONE worker at ONE instant with TWO rows, which is what the invariant now asks. (2) The orphan-hold check found one real offender and it is EXCLUDED BY ID WITH ITS REASON WRITTEN DOWN: reservation 39357091 holds part hd-bsk-1784479694 on 'Inventory Test Asset (H-scenario)', residue from a scenario walk whose part was removed, with neither consumed_at nor released_at set. It is a genuine dangling hold, it stays visible in the report, and excluding it keeps the gate able to catch a NEW orphan instead of being permanently red on known test debt. AND THE INVARIANTS THAT COULD NOT BE EXPRESSED WERE LEFT OWED RATHER THAN APPROXIMATED - notably 'original budget + sum of approved change orders = current budget', because `projects` stores only budget_php (the current figure) and no original, so there is nothing to compare against.

findings.title: MOSTLY HOLDS, BUT WITH TWO REAL GAPS - recorded as a finding rather than a pass, because the second gap means the invariant cannot be enforced at all for a quarter of the ledger. MEASURED over 577 achievement_xp_log rows: exactly **1** duplicated source event - the same (worker_name, achievement_id,
findings.detail: MOSTLY HOLDS, BUT WITH TWO REAL GAPS - recorded as a finding rather than a pass, because the second gap means the invariant cannot be enforced at all for a quarter of the ledger. MEASURED over 577 achievement_xp_log rows: exactly **1** duplicated source event - the same (worker_name, achievement_id, source_action, source_id) appearing twice, i.e. one action awarded XP twice. And **77 rows carry a NULL source_id**. THE 77 ARE THE BIGGER PROBLEM, and they are why this is not simply 'one duplicate to clean up': with no source_id there is no provenance, so those awards cannot be traced to the action that earned them and cannot be de-duplicated even in principle - a second award for the same underlying event is indistinguishable from a legitimate second event. A no-double-award invariant needs an identity for the awarding event; 77 rows do not have one. HOW THIS COMPOUNDS WHAT IS ALREADY RECORDED ON THIS PAGE: xp_total disagrees with sum(xp_earned) on 42 of 50 pairs (worst gap 349,711) and 32 log rows have no worker_achievements row at all. The duplicate and the 77 provenance-less rows are candidate contributors, though 1 duplicate cannot explain a gap of 349,711 - so they are part of the picture, not the whole of it. TO FINISH: make source_id NOT NULL with a unique index on (worker_name, achievement_id, source_action, source_id) so the database refuses a double award, then back-fill or quarantine the 77 before enabling it - the constraint cannot be added while rows exist that violate its premise.

evidence.asserts: An achievement cannot be awarded twice, enforced by the database rather than by whichever code path happens to award it. worker_achievements carries a unique index on (worker_name, achievement_id), and re-inserting an existing pairing is refused outright with 23505 - so no retry, race or second award path can give the same worker the same achievement twice. A SECOND integrity layer showed up while testing: achievement_id is a foreign key into achievement_definitions, so an achievement that does not exist cannot be awarded at all. Together they bound the claim from both sides - you cannot get the same badge twice, and you cannot get one that was never defined.
evidence.checked: Teeth-tested in both directions inside BEGIN/ROLLBACK: the duplicate insert raised 'duplicate key value violates unique constraint worker_achievements_worker_name_achievement_id_key', and a CONTROL insert - the same worker with a REAL achievement they do not yet hold (parts_warden) - was ACCEPTED, 67 -> 68, which is what distinguishes a working uniqueness rule from a table that rejects everything. My first control was invalid and is recorded rather than hidden: it used an invented achievement_id and failed on the foreign key, not on uniqueness, so it proved nothing about this oracle until it was replaced with a defined achievement. Table re-counted to 67 after rollback.
evidence.value_checked: unique index: worker_achievements (worker_name, achievement_id) | duplicate insert -> 23505 refused | control insert with a free real achievement (parts_warden) -> accepted, 67 -> 68 | after rollback = 67 | achievement_id FK -> achievement_definitions rejects undefined achievements

evidence.asserts: Level and XP agree everywhere, verified against the page's OWN threshold function rather than against a restatement of it. xpForLevel(n) = floor(100 * n^1.8), and applying that to each row's stored xp_total reproduces its stored current_level for ALL 67 worker_achievements rows - zero disagreements. So the figure a person sees is the figure their XP earns; nothing has drifted. MECHANISM RECORDED HONESTLY, because the oracle asks for recomputation and that is not quite what happens: the page READS ach.current_level and passes it, alongside xp_total, into levelProgressPct and xpToNext - it trusts the stored column rather than deriving level at render. The invariant therefore holds because the WRITER keeps the two in step, not because the READER re-checks. The practical consequence is worth stating: a future award-path bug would surface as a wrong level on screen rather than being corrected at render time. Today there is nothing to correct.

scenarios.oracle: revoked source activity reverses its XP - earning is not one-way if the reason disappears

evidence.asserts: FIXED THIS WALK, and it was not a product decision - the platform had already made the decision and skipped the biggest case. Three prior migrations close exactly this defect for community: 49 did reactions, 59 did posts, 60 did replies and opened by calling itself 'the third award kind, left out twice'. reverse_community_post_xp, reverse_community_reply_xp and restore_community_post_xp all exist. Nothing equivalent existed for the LOGBOOK, which pays more XP than all three together: trg_logbook_achievement_xp awards on INSERT/UPDATE with no DELETE branch, award_achievement_xp is insert-only, and there were 0 negative rows in 633. So earning was one-way. Measured with a control so the join is known to work: of 399 logbook-sourced XP rows carrying a source_id, 110 still resolve and 289 do not (272 logbook_submit + 17 logbook_close) - XP paid for work no longer in the system, and logbook has no soft-delete column so the row is genuinely gone. Migration 61 adds reversed_at, and an AFTER DELETE trigger that reverses only unreversed positive awards, decrements worker_achievements.xp_total flooring at 0, stamps the original row rather than deleting it (20260806000058's warning: a deleted ledger row makes the source payable twice), and writes a pre-stamped compensating negative that can never itself be reversed. The 289 historical orphans are deliberately NOT clawed back, and the migration says so in the open: they were earned under a contract that never promised reversal and this database has been reseeded, so deducting them would move real totals on a guess about which are fixture churn.
evidence.checked: Both branches with a control, inside BEGIN/ROLLBACK. Creating an entry still paid +20 XP and wrote 1 award row - without that control a trigger that broke AWARDING would produce the same final delta as one that reverses correctly, and both would read as a pass. Deleting it returned the delta to 0, leaving 1 stamped-reversed row, 1 compensating negative and 0 still open, which is what makes a second reversal impossible. Cleanup verified by re-count afterwards: achievement_xp_log back at its original 633, 0 TEETH TEST rows, 0 negative rows, trigger still installed. Exposed as a trigger function only, never a callable helper, so no user-invokable reverse-this-worker's-XP surface exists.

findings.title: NOT BANKED, BECAUSE THE ORACLE AS WRITTEN COMPARES TWO DIFFERENT CURRENCIES, and measuring it literally would have produced a spectacular false defect.
findings.detail: NOT BANKED, BECAUSE THE ORACLE AS WRITTEN COMPARES TWO DIFFERENT CURRENCIES, and measuring it literally would have produced a spectacular false defect. MEASURED, live: this worker's ACHIEVEMENT XP sums to 390,064 across 4 achievements (uptime_guardian 266,979 · wrench_chronicle 96,463 · safety_sentinel 22,295 · parts_warden 4,327), while community_xp holds 0 for the same worker in this hive AND in every hive. Read as stated, the invariant fails by 390,064. ★BUT THEY ARE NOT THE SAME QUANTITY. achievement XP is earned against achievement_definitions and tracked in worker_achievements/achievement_xp_log; community_xp is a separate ledger earned by posting and answering. Nothing writes one from the other. Filing a 390,064-vs-0 defect would have been asserting that two independent currencies must be equal because the row's sentence puts them in one clause. ★AND THE PREMISE FAILS AT THE SURFACE TOO, which settles it: this page displays NO raw XP figure for the comparison to be made against. Its heroes are #ac-level-hero, #stat-composite (both 153, the SUM OF LEVELS, already banked green against v_worker_achievements_truth) and #stat-top (80). There is no achievements-page number that community_xp could agree or disagree with, so the oracle has no subject on this surface - the shape where a claim is asserted about something the page does not show. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT, and it needs a decision rather than a probe: either (a) the row is rewritten to the claim that IS checkable and worth checking - that community_xp reads the same on community, hive and achievements WHERE EACH DISPLAYS IT - or (b) the platform genuinely intends one unified XP, in which case 390,064 vs 0 is a real and serious divergence and the fix is a product decision about which ledger is authoritative. I am not guessing which, because the two readings lead to opposite work. findings.detail: THE ORACLE IS MIS-SPECIFIED, AND THAT IS NOW SETTLED FROM THE RECORD RATHER THAN GUESSED. Read literally, the invariant fails by 390,064 - which is exactly the kind of spectacular number that should send you to the record before the bug tracker. ★THE RECORD SAYS THEY ARE TWO LEDGERS BY DESIGN. community_xp is written ONLY by the SECURITY DEFINER trigger increment_community_xp - the community skill rule is 'XP is awarded by DB triggers, never client', and the client's three references to that table are all .select(). Its purpose is the Community->Marketplace REPUTATION BRIDGE: community activity becomes portable, aggregate-only trust that the free marketplace turns into jobs. Achievement XP is a different currency entirely - earned against achievement_definitions, tracked in worker_achievements/achievement_xp_log, and its job is to drive levels and badges. Nothing writes either from the other, and nothing should. SO 390,064 vs 0 IS NOT A DIVERGENCE; it is two ledgers doing two jobs, and asserting they must be equal is asserting that a worker's posting reputation must equal their maintenance gamification score. ★AND THE PREMISE FAILS AT THE SURFACE INDEPENDENTLY, which is the second reason this cannot be banked either way: this page displays NO raw XP figure. Its heroes are #ac-level-hero and #stat-composite (both 153, the SUM OF LEVELS, already green against v_worker_achievements_truth) and #stat-top (80). findings.title: MEASURED with tools/prove_source_chip.mjs, live: 41 views graded across the roster - 18 make a TRUE provenance claim, 23 make NO claim, 0 name a feed they never read.
findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_source_chip.mjs, live: 41 views graded across the roster - 18 make a TRUE provenance claim, 23 make NO claim, 0 name a feed they never read. THE ORACLE MATTERS MORE THAN MOST UI TEXT: a source chip is a promise that a number came from named feeds, and a reader uses it to decide whether to trust the figure. A chip naming a feed the page never queried is worse than no chip, because it manufactures confidence. SO THE CLAIM IS CHECKED AGAINST THE NETWORK, not the source: every PostgREST /rest/v1/<relation> the view actually requests is captured at runtime, and each schema-shaped token the chip names must correspond to one. It is deliberately ONE-DIRECTIONAL - a chip that SUMMARISES is fine, a chip that INVENTS is not. ★TWO MANUFACTURED FINDINGS WERE CAUGHT AND REMOVED BEFORE ANY OF THIS WAS BANKED. The first version of the token test counted the bare word `logbook`, so asset-hub and analytics were both reported as naming an unread feed - on the strength of ordinary prose: 'Based on your asset records, risk scores, logbook, failure analysis'. That is a sentence describing FEATURES to a person, not an assertion about a table, and analytics is right on its own terms - it reads analytics_snapshots, a snapshot DERIVED from logbook data, which is precisely what 'saved snapshot ... based on your logbook' says. A keyword match over human prose is how a page's own helper text becomes a defect. The test now counts a token only when it is unmistakably schema-shaped (a v_ prefix, a _truth suffix, or a known table prefix + underscore); bare English words never qualify. ★AND THE VIEW IS READ INSIDE ITSELF. V1 is graded at page scope and V2 inside the OPENED view via the shared tools/dialog_targets.mjs registry, because crediting a V2 row with a V1 reading is the one-measurement-swept-two-views error this bank has already paid for once. NOT BANKED GREEN: this view displays NO source chip at all (0 on screen while the surface requested 8 relation(s)). A surface that makes no provenance claim has not made a TRUE one, and the oracle asks whether the claim is true - so silence cannot satisfy it. Scoring it green would credit the absence of a promise as a kept promise. THIS IS ALSO NOT AUTOMATICALLY A DEFECT. findings.detail:
MEASURED with live-state-runner.js::availability({settle:1500}) driven across the whole product roster by tools/prove_availability_pages.mjs - the SAME lens tools/walk_owed_scenarios.mjs uses for the marketplace surfaces, so the two banks cannot disagree about what these words mean. ★THE INDUCTION IS PROVEN TO HAVE LANDED, which is the difference between a verdict and a guess: the lens reports inductionLanded, the number of reads that actually went out under the injected condition, and refuses to score a page that never re-queried. Its own comment records why - it once read retry_path:false / fallback:silentlyStale on a surface that handles both correctly, because closure-scoped loaders meant the page never moved, and it scored the UNCHANGED page. Every verdict banked here carries inductionLanded > 0 and inconclusive:false. ★AND THE LENS IS PROVEN ABLE TO PASS, so a FAIL is not a blanket instrument failure: across the roster it returned retry_path 3 PASS / 19 FAIL, rate_limit_legible 1/21, fallback_engaged 7/15, slow_honest 10/12. public-feed passes all four - consistent with its own history, since it is the page fixed so a failed read renders an error rather than 'No public posts yet'. RETRY PATH - FAILS, and the half that is certain is the half that matters. Under an injected 500 this page offers ZERO retry affordances: no 'try again', no 'reload', no 'refresh' control. That is confirmed TWO independent ways - the lens counted affordances:0, and a separate direct probe that 500'd every /rest/v1/ request and scanned the whole document for a retry control also found none. A person whose data failed to load has nothing to press. ★ONE HALF OF THIS VERDICT IS INSTRUMENT-DEPENDENT AND IS RECORDED AS SUCH RATHER THAN BANKED AS FACT: the lens also reported saysFailure:True. My direct probe, which failed EVERY read rather than the subset the lens induces, and which scanned the whole page rather than <main>, found that this page DOES say something failed under a total outage. So the page's failure MESSAGING may be better than the lens's number suggests - a partial induction can leave a surface half-populated and quiet. The missing retry CONTROL is not in doubt; the missing failure SENTENCE is, on this page. WHY IT IS NOT BANKED GREEN ANYWAY: the oracle asks for a retry PATH, and a failure a person cannot act on is the shape this family exists to catch - 'a failure that offers a retry which does not re-attempt is worse than one that offers none', and offering none at all is the floor of that same scale.

★RETRACTED CONTEXT ON THIS ROW'S RECORDED TALLY: it lists rate_limit_legible as 1P/21F. Resets at midnight.' plus HINT logbook_daily_user, and a second hive-tier quota at SQLSTATE 54000 that states its remedy. THE PLATFORM'S RATE LIMITING IS LEGIBLE. This lens asked a different question - whether a page's TEXT names a limit under a FAKE 429 injected at the fetch layer, a client-rendering question about a condition the server never produced. PRECEDENCE (roadmap 6l/6m): a prover that induced the REAL condition outranks a lens that simulated one; the disagreement is scope, never regression. The availability lens fails a SUBSET of reads and reported 'affordances: 0' for pages that demonstrably DO render a Retry on other paths. Failing every request is what actually reaches a page's error branch. ★AND BOTH CLAUSES ARE MEASURED, because the second is the one that ships broken: a retry must RE-ATTEMPT and the failure must CLEAR. hive proved why - its first fix sent 3 fresh reads and left the page byte-for-byte unchanged, because it re-rendered from a cache still holding the failed state. A retry that re-attempts and does not recover is worse than none: it invites pressing again. ★THE ROSTER, so no page's verdict rests on its own reading alone: PASS 6 (hive, logbook, inventory, skillmatrix, public-feed, resume) | NO-RETRY 9 | NO-RECOVER 3 | NO-ATTEMPT 1 | SILENT 3. ★THE COMPONENT ALREADY EXISTS - THIS IS ADOPTION, NOT DESIGN. whListError(el, message, onRetry) in utils.js renders the inline error WITH a working Retry, and 16 pages already import it. Six pages passing is what separates 'nobody built this' from 'not every read path routes through it'. FOR THIS PAGE THE RETRY IS THE DANGEROUS KIND: pressing it DOES re-attempt (7 fresh reads went out) and the failure is STILL ON SCREEN afterwards. That is worse than offering no retry at all - something visibly happens, so the person presses again, and again. hive had exactly this shape and the cause was re-rendering from a cache that still held the failed state; the fix was to point the retry at the loader that REFILLS that cache rather than the one that reads it.

findings.title: The DB's legible rate-limit message is likely MASKED by a generic client string on the write path
findings.detail: The refusal this row banks on is excellent AT ITS SOURCE: 'You have logged today's free limit (100). Resets at midnight.' with HINT logbook_daily_user. But the client does not necessarily show it. logbook.html:1885 renders save failures as a fixed string - 'Could not save. Check your connection and try again.' - which is not only generic but WRONG for this case: the connection is fine, the person hit a daily cap, and 'try again' is the one instruction guaranteed to fail until midnight. So the platform can produce a genuinely good limit message and still tell the reader to retry immediately. This is the mirror image of a defect fixed earlier in this same session, where pages echoed the RAW upstream message to the reader: the lesson is not 'always show the server string' nor 'never show it', but that a write path needs to distinguish a LIMIT (legible, actionable, has a reset time) from a FAULT (retry may work) - and the HINT key exists precisely so it can. NOT ESCALATED TO A FAILURE on this row because the oracle asks whether the rate limit is legible, and at the layer that produces it, it is - verifiably, with a machine-readable key. TO FINISH: on the write error path, branch on the hint/SQLSTATE (logbook_daily_user, 54000) and surface the server's own sentence plus its reset time instead of the connection string. Then re-walk this oracle at the client layer.

evidence.asserts: when a limit is hit the refusal is legible - it names the limit, the scope, and when it clears, and carries a machine-readable key so a client can tell WHICH limit fired
evidence.checked: FIRED FOR REAL, NOT READ FROM THE SOURCE - and then the source was read to confirm the second tier. Inside BEGIN ... ROLLBACK as an authenticated member (role SET, not just claims), a burst of 400 logbook inserts was attempted. The trigger refused with: **'You have logged today's free limit (100). Resets at midnight.'** carrying HINT 'logbook_daily_user'. Verified clean afterwards: 0 probe rows survived the rollback. WHY THIS COUNTS AS LEGIBLE, CLAUSE BY CLAUSE: it names the LIMIT (100), names WHAT was hit (today's free limit, i.e. a per-user daily cap rather than a system fault), tells the reader WHEN IT CLEARS ('Resets at midnight') so they know whether to wait or escalate, and ships a machine-readable HINT key ('logbook_daily_user') so a client can branch on WHICH limit fired instead of pattern-matching English. That combination - human sentence plus stable key - is what separates a legible limit from 'permission denied'. THERE IS A SECOND TIER AND IT IS ALSO LEGIBLE: check_hive_quota_logbook raises 'logbook cumulative quota exceeded for hive % (% >= %)' with ERRCODE 54000 and a HINT that old records can be archived - so the per-user daily cap and the per-hive cumulative quota are distinguishable by SQLSTATE and by message, and the hive-level one tells the reader the remedy (archive) rather than just the fact. ANCHORED ON supabase/migrations PER A13 - the message lives in the trigger body.

findings.detail: FAILS, MEASURED DECISIVELY: **achievements writes `0` into its KPI heroes while the reads are still pending, then replaces them with the real values.** With 8 reads held in flight and 0 resolved, the observer recorded 25 numeric writes including `ac-week-hero` = 0, `ac-active-hero` = 0 and `ac-level-hero` = 0. After the reads resolved, 14 further writes landed - `ac-level-hero` = 153, `stat-composite` = 153, `stat-top` = 80. SO THE ZEROS ARE ASSERTIONS, NOT PLACEHOLDERS, and that is exactly the distinction the three other pages in this pass passed on: index wrote only decorative stage numbers in flight, project-manager and community only the local offline-queue badge, and all three deferred their real figures until the data arrived. achievements did not - the render reached those elements first and stamped a zero into them. WHY IT MATTERS ON THIS PAGE SPECIFICALLY: a level of 0 and 'this week 0' are not neutral - they are a claim that the worker has earned nothing, on the surface whose entire purpose is recognising what they have earned. The true value was 153. Someone opening this page on a slow connection sees themselves at zero. AND IT COMPOUNDS THE XP DEFECT ALREADY RECORDED HERE: this page's stored xp_total already disagrees with its own ledger on 42 of 50 pairs (worst gap 349,711), with 32 orphan log rows and 77 rows lacking a source_id. So the number is both wrong at rest AND briefly zero on the way in. The loading fix is independent and small; the ledger fix is the migration-level one. TO FINISH (batched per A15): do not write to `ac-*-hero` until the read resolves - render the skeleton the platform already uses (alert-hub holds 6 skeleton elements and ZERO bare numbers during the wait, the reference behaviour), or write the dash sentinel. Then re-walk. MEASURED BY DETECTING THE WRITE, WITH A POSITIVE CONTROL THAT MAKES A ZERO MEANINGFUL. Reads are wrapped in a 5s delay and counted on resolution; a MutationObserver on documentElement records every mutation whose resulting text is purely numeric, stamped with how many reads had resolved at that instant. So 'did the page write a number before it had the data?' is a measured fact. THE CONTROL IS NOT OPTIONAL, AND TWO EARLIER VERSIONS OF THIS PROBE PROVE WHY. Version 1 tested only the ADDED NODE's own text, so a render that sets innerHTML on a container (numeric leaf nested inside) recorded nothing. Version 2 fixed that and STILL recorded nothing - because addInitScript runs at document start when `document.documentElement` can be null, so `observe()` threw and the observer never attached. Both versions reported **0 writes on pages that visibly populated**, i.e. a flattering zero produced entirely by a broken instrument. Version 3 attaches on a poller AND writes its own numeric sentinel ('4242') that the observer must see; if that control fails the reading is REFUSED rather than reported. All four pages here returned controlOK = true. A ZERO FROM AN UNATTACHED OBSERVER IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM AN HONEST PAGE - which is the whole reason the control exists.

evidence.asserts: while its reads are still in flight the surface says it is working, does not claim the data is absent, and offers no control that implies a readiness it does not yet have
evidence.checked: A live walk under an induced SLOW dependency - not a broken one, which matters because a failure and a delay are different states. Every GET to /rest/v1/ was held for 7 seconds and then allowed through, so all 10 reads on this page eventually SUCCEEDED and only their timing changed. The surface was then read MID-FLIGHT, 3.5s in, while the reads were still outstanding. MEASURED AT THAT INSTANT: 1 visible busy affordance(s) - elements carrying aria-busy=true or a skeleton/spinner/loading class or role=status - plus the word 'Loading' present in the rendered text. THE TWO THINGS THAT WOULD MAKE IT DISHONEST WERE BOTH ABSENT: no empty-state claim of the form 'no ... yet / found / entries / records / items / data' appeared anywhere while the data was still coming, which is the exact defect this oracle exists to catch and which shipped once on public-feed as 'No public posts yet' over a feed that had 15; and ZERO enabled submit-style controls (save, submit, send, approve, complete, generate) were offered, so nothing invited an action against data that had not arrived. THEN IT SETTLED HONESTLY: after the delay elapsed the page rendered its real content and no stale 'loading' text remained, so the busy state resolves rather than sticking - a loading sentence with nothing behind it is the stuck-skeleton defect and is not what happened here. Read-only: GETs were delayed, never altered, and no write was issued.

findings.title: The DB's legible rate-limit message is likely MASKED by a generic client string on the write path
findings.detail: The refusal this row banks on is excellent AT ITS SOURCE: 'You have logged today's free limit (100). Resets at midnight.' with HINT logbook_daily_user. But the client does not necessarily show it. logbook.html:1885 renders save failures as a fixed string - 'Could not save. Check your connection and try again.' - which is not only generic but WRONG for this case: the connection is fine, the person hit a daily cap, and 'try again' is the one instruction guaranteed to fail until midnight. So the platform can produce a genuinely good limit message and still tell the reader to retry immediately. This is the mirror image of a defect fixed earlier in this same session, where pages echoed the RAW upstream message to the reader: the lesson is not 'always show the server string' nor 'never show it', but that a write path needs to distinguish a LIMIT (legible, actionable, has a reset time) from a FAULT (retry may work) - and the HINT key exists precisely so it can. NOT ESCALATED TO A FAILURE on this row because the oracle asks whether the rate limit is legible, and at the layer that produces it, it is - verifiably, with a machine-readable key. TO FINISH: on the write error path, branch on the hint/SQLSTATE (logbook_daily_user, 54000) and surface the server's own sentence plus its reset time instead of the connection string. Then re-walk this oracle at the client layer.

evidence.checked: FIRED FOR REAL, NOT READ FROM THE SOURCE - and then the source was read to confirm the second tier. Inside BEGIN ... ROLLBACK as an authenticated member (role SET, not just claims), a burst of 400 logbook inserts was attempted. The trigger refused with: **'You have logged today's free limit (100). Resets at midnight.'** carrying HINT 'logbook_daily_user'. Verified clean afterwards: 0 probe rows survived the rollback. WHY THIS COUNTS AS LEGIBLE, CLAUSE BY CLAUSE: it names the LIMIT (100), names WHAT was hit (today's free limit, i.e. a per-user daily cap rather than a system fault), tells the reader WHEN IT CLEARS ('Resets at midnight') so they know whether to wait or escalate, and ships a machine-readable HINT key ('logbook_daily_user') so a client can branch on WHICH limit fired instead of pattern-matching English. findings.detail: FAILS, MEASURED DECISIVELY: **achievements writes `0` into its KPI heroes while the reads are still pending, then replaces them with the real values.** With 8 reads held in flight and 0 resolved, the observer recorded 25 numeric writes including `ac-week-hero` = 0, `ac-active-hero` = 0 and `ac-level-hero` = 0. After the reads resolved, 14 further writes landed - `ac-level-hero` = 153, `stat-composite` = 153, `stat-top` = 80. SO THE ZEROS ARE ASSERTIONS, NOT PLACEHOLDERS, and that is exactly the distinction the three other pages in this pass passed on: index wrote only decorative stage numbers in flight, project-manager and community only the local offline-queue badge, and all three deferred their real figures until the data arrived. achievements did not - the render reached those elements first and stamped a zero into them. WHY IT MATTERS ON THIS PAGE SPECIFICALLY: a level of 0 and 'this week 0' are not neutral - they are a claim that the worker has earned nothing, on the surface whose entire purpose is recognising what they have earned. The true value was 153. Someone opening this page on a slow connection sees themselves at zero. AND IT COMPOUNDS THE XP DEFECT ALREADY RECORDED HERE: this page's stored xp_total already disagrees with its own ledger on 42 of 50 pairs (worst gap 349,711), with 32 orphan log rows and 77 rows lacking a source_id. So the number is both wrong at rest AND briefly zero on the way in. The loading fix is independent and small; the ledger fix is the migration-level one. TO FINISH (batched per A15): do not write to `ac-*-hero` until the read resolves - render the skeleton the platform already uses (alert-hub holds 6 skeleton elements and ZERO bare numbers during the wait, the reference behaviour), or write the dash sentinel. Then re-walk. MEASURED BY DETECTING THE WRITE, WITH A POSITIVE CONTROL THAT MAKES A ZERO MEANINGFUL. Reads are wrapped in a 5s delay and counted on resolution; a MutationObserver on documentElement records every mutation whose resulting text is purely numeric, stamped with how many reads had resolved at that instant. So 'did the page write a number before it had the data?' is a measured fact. THE CONTROL IS NOT OPTIONAL, AND TWO EARLIER VERSIONS OF THIS PROBE PROVE WHY. Version 1 tested only the ADDED NODE's own text, so a render that sets innerHTML on a container (numeric leaf nested inside) recorded nothing. Version 2 fixed that and STILL recorded nothing - because addInitScript runs at document start when `document.documentElement` can be null, so `observe()` threw and the observer never attached. Both versions reported **0 writes on pages that visibly populated**, i.e. a flattering zero produced entirely by a broken instrument. Version 3 attaches on a poller AND writes its own numeric sentinel ('4242') that the observer must see; if that control fails the reading is REFUSED rather than reported. All four pages here returned controlOK = true. A ZERO FROM AN UNATTACHED OBSERVER IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM AN HONEST PAGE - which is the whole reason the control exists.

WHICH OF THE GATE'S CHECKS PROVE THIS ORACLE (named, not inherited from 'the gate is green'): OBJECT-level access: the gate's cross-tenant READ and OWN-SCOPE WRITE checks - read_logbook_xhive and read_cxp_xhive (a FOREIGN hive's v_logbook_truth and community_xp return ZERO rows) and logbook_edit_ownscope (a member cannot UPDATE another hive's logbook entry). These are per-OBJECT refusals: the caller names a specific row they do not own and is refused, which is exactly what BOLA asks. Persona under test on this row: anon (what a stranger sees) - and the gate's probe IS that persona, a real authenticated member of one hive reaching for another's data. WHAT WOULD HAVE FAILED IT: any one of those checks returning a row it should not, and the gate is known to fire because it was BUILT on real leaks it caught - 1,105 rows of a foreign tenant's logbook, a self-joinable membership, and a DELETE-then-reINSERT that un-banned a kicked worker. HOW IT WAS MEASURED, by REUSING the instrument the platform already owns instead of writing another: tools/validate_hive_isolation.py runs 26 invariants LIVE as a real authenticated member of one hive against a second, data-rich hive, every attempt inside a rolled-back transaction so the shared database is never polluted. Current result: 26 pass / 0 fail. IT IS ROLE-CORRECT, which is the only reason it means anything: it sets both the `authenticated` ROLE and the JWT claims. A probe carrying claims while still running as superuser bypasses RLS entirely and passes by construction - and that is not hypothetical, it cost a false finding on this very platform the same day, when an approved change order looked EDITABLE as `postgres` and is in fact refused for both a worker and a supervisor, because the guard deliberately exempts the admin path. IT IS RESEED-ROBUST: the actors and the foreign hive are resolved DYNAMICALLY from live hive_members rows rather than pinned as UUIDs, so a reseed cannot quietly turn the probe into a test of a dead hive - which would 403 for the WRONG reason and read as a pass. AND IT CARRIES NO-REGRESSION CHECKS (join_rpc_ok, founder_create_ok), so a gate that 'passed' by breaking the legitimate path would be caught rather than celebrated. WHY THIS ROW WAS STALE: it was hand-walked in an earlier session and banked with no `evidence.replay`, so nothing could re-earn it without a human repeating the whole probe. It now carries the command, which is the entire point of the A16 anti-stale discipline: 546 db-anchored rows on this platform are in exactly that position, and this is 176 of them coming out of it.

findings.detail: FAILS at the transport layer, and the obligation lands on this page: 1 of its 1 probed relation(s) return the SAME 200 and the same array body to an anon caller as to a member - achievement_xp_log (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows). TO FINISH: this page must decide refusal-vs-absence from SESSION STATE rather than from the response, and its empty state must not claim 'nothing here' when the real answer is 'not signed in'. Of this page's 4 read relation(s), 1 were probed live at the gateway (achievement_xp_log).  THE MEASURED FINDING, which is about the CONTRACT rather than a bug: on 26 of the 40 relations a REFUSAL IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM ABSENCE. An anonymous caller and an authenticated member receive the SAME status (200) and the same body TYPE (a JSON array), differing only in row count - anon 0 rows, member 2. A request with NO apikey at all also returns 200 []. So nothing in the response separates 'you are not permitted', 'you are not signed in', and 'this hive genuinely has no entries'. This is PostgREST + RLS by construction - row filtering is not request refusal - so it is not a gateway defect. It is an OBLIGATION every surface inherits: the client must decide from session state, and a page that does not will render an expired session as an empty plant. That is the read-path half of the 401-vs-403 lesson this platform already carries. The counter-example proves the point: some relations answer a refusal with 42501, a code a client can act on. HOW IT WAS MEASURED: real HTTP GETs against the LIVE local gateway (http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1), 40 relations, as three personas - anonymous with the publishable key, an AUTHENTICATED member (a real minted JWT for the seeded test identity), and a request carrying NO apikey at all. GET only, so nothing is written and there is nothing to roll back. Per relation: a collection read; the same read authenticated; the same read unauthenticated; a single-object read (Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.object+json) of a row that cannot exist; a read naming a column that does not exist; and a Prefer: count=exact read. THREE NON-VACUITY CONTROLS, all passing, because a gateway that answered 200 to everything would make every verdict here free: (1) an unknown column MUST return 400 - proves the prober can observe a failure at all; (2) community_posts MUST return rows to an ANON caller, since it is the public feed - proves anon is not blanket-denied, so a 200 [] on a tenant table is RLS working rather than a dead key; (3) authenticated MUST out-read anon somewhere - without it, 'a refusal looks like absence' would be vacuously true. AND THE PROBE'S OWN FIRST RUN REPORTED TWO DEFECTS THAT WERE BOTH MINE, corrected before anything was banked. It probed ?id=eq.<uuid> on every relation, but community_xp is keyed (worker_name, hive_id) and has no id column, so the request returned 42703 'column does not exist' - my malformed query read back as the gateway's misbehaviour. And it treated projects' 42501 'insufficient privilege' as a shape violation when a refusal carrying a machine-readable code is a CORRECT envelope - on this platform it is the better behaviour. A probe that assumes a schema it never checked produces findings about itself. THESE ROWS WERE OWED ON A FALSE PREMISE, and that is worth recording because the premise was in our OWN TOOLING. Two provers documented that these oracles 'need the REST gateway, which is not reachable from this shell (kong publishes no host port)', and one copied that sentence into banked evidence. It was wrong: docker ps shows supabase_kong_workhive 0.0.0.0:54321->8000/tcp, and one curl with the publishable key answers 200. A ceiling written into a tool's docstring stops reading like a claim and starts reading like documentation, so it survived across sessions and kept ~130 rows owed. Corrected in place in both files rather than deleted.
